title: Pillow CVE-2026-112900: How to find and fix it with GitLab
summary: Upgrade to Pillow 13.0.0, then use dependency scanning, code search, and GitLab Duo Agent Platform to patch every affected Python project in your groups.
body_markdown:
> **GitLab is not affected by CVE-2026-112900 or the other vulnerabilities fixed in Pillow 13.0.0. GitLab products do not include the Pillow library, and our Security team has found no evidence of impact to GitLab-managed infrastructure. GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated are not impacted.**


Pillow is one of the most widely used image libraries in the Python ecosystem. It often sits several layers down in a dependency tree, pulled in by a web framework, a thumbnailing service or an ML toolkit that nobody chose it for directly. On October 16, 2026, the Pillow project released[version 13.0.0](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/13.0.0.html) , and one of its security fixes is[CVE-2026-112900](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-112900) : an argument injection in the way Pillow calls Ghostscript to render EPS images. The CVE record, published on October 19, rates it 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. It affects every Pillow release from 2.6.0 up to, but not including, 13.0.0. No exploitation in the wild has been reported so far, but CISA's assessment marks it as automatable with total technical impact.


**Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 on every project and image that handles untrusted images, and remove Ghostscript from images that do not need EPS support.**


**This guide is for security and platform teams with Python projects on GitLab** . It covers the fixed version for each distribution, how the flaw works, the other High and Critical issues fixed in the same release, how to locate affected projects with[dependency scanning](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/dependency_scanning/dependency_scanning_sbom/) ,[container scanning](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/container_scanning/) ,[GitLab Orbit](https://docs.gitlab.com/orbit/) , and[code search](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/search/exact_code_search/) , and how to remediate at scale with[GitLab Duo Agent Platform](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/) .


## CVE-2026-112900 at a glance


CVE-2026-112900 is an OS command and argument injection flaw in Pillow's EPS plugin, rated Critical (CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2) by the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA). The[CVE record](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-112900) was published on October 19, 2026.


Field Detail


CVE CVE-2026-112900


GitHub advisory[GHSA-w889-685w-c8fh](https://github.com/python-pillow/Pillow/security/advisories/GHSA-w889-685w-c8fh)


Title Pillow: Argument Injection in Ghostscript call, potentially leading into RCE


Weakness CWE-88 (argument injection), CWE-78 (OS command injection)


CVSS 4.0 9.2 Critical (AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H)


Affected versions Pillow >= 2.6.0 and < 13.0.0


Fixed in Pillow 13.0.0


Exploitation status None known at the time of writing ([CISA SSVC assessment](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-112900) dated October 20, 2026)


## Upgrade Pillow to a fixed version now


Upgrade Pillow to 13.0.0 or later. The CVE record lists 13.0.0 as the only fixed version, so every older branch needs to move to it. Framework updates and input validation on image contents do not help here, because the flaw is in how the filename reaches Ghostscript.


Your Python version What to do


3.11 to 3.15 Upgrade with` pip install --upgrade "pillow>=13.0.0"` , or raise the pin in your lockfile or requirements file.


**If your Pillow comes from a distribution package, check the distribution's tracker first.** Distribution packages keep their own version numbers, so compare against the tracker instead of` pip show` . Status as of October 26, 2026:

Amazon Linux 2 is listed as not affected. Ubuntu lists all releases as needing evaluation, and Red Hat, Arch Linux and Oracle Linux had no record for this CVE. Alpine's tracker could not be checked.*


Until your distribution ships a fix, install Pillow 13.0.0 from PyPI in a virtual environment or container, or apply the workarounds below.


**Rebuild your container images.** If your Dockerfile installs Pillow without pinning a patch version, rebuild it with` docker build --pull --no-cache` and redeploy it so the install step resolves the fixed release. Images that pin a version, such as` pillow==12.3.0` , need the pin changed first. Images built on top of other base images only get the fix once their maintainers update them, so check the upstream image before you rebuild.


Pillow 13.0.0 also changes a few behaviors, such as how duplicate TIFF tags are handled and how I-mode images are saved as PNG, so run your image-processing tests before you ship the upgrade.


## How the vulnerability works


EPS files are PostScript programs, so Pillow shells out to Ghostscript (` gs` ) to render them, passing the input filename right after` -f` with no sanitizing.


When the image object has a` .name` that exists on disk, Pillow used that name as-is. Ghostscript's argument parser gives two kinds of strings special meaning:


- **A leading` -`** is read as an option rather than a filename, which gives an attacker argument injection (CWE-88).
- **A leading` @`** tells Ghostscript to read more command-line arguments from the named text file. If the attacker also controls that file's contents, they control additional Ghostscript arguments, which is the path toward command execution (CWE-78).


The advisory notes that this works even with` -dSAFER` , the sandbox flag Pillow passes by default. That flag restricts what a PostScript program can do, but it does not stop an attacker from injecting arguments into the command line itself.


## How to check if you are affected


You are exposed only if all of these are true:


1. Pillow is below 13.0.0.
2. Ghostscript is installed.
3. Your code opens an EPS file by a filename an attacker can influence, such as an upload saved under its original name.
4. The image is loaded or rendered, not just opened.


Full command execution also needs the attacker to control a text file referenced with a leading` @` . Services that generate their own filenames or use in-memory streams are far less likely to be reachable.


**If you cannot upgrade yet:** save uploads under generated names, restrict formats with` Image.open(f, formats=\["PNG", "JPEG"\])` , or remove Ghostscript from images that do not need it.

The two that do not, GHSA-xcvg-w56q-r89m and GHSA-78g4-xqwv-q3g8, are worth watching, because tools that match only on CVE IDs would miss them.

## Locate Pillow across your GitLab groups


Find every project that installs Pillow, then fix first the ones that also have Ghostscript and accept uploads.


1. **Dependency scanning** reports the Pillow version in your lockfiles, including transitive dependencies.[Turn it on](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/dependency_scanning/dependency_scanning_sbom/) per project, or for a whole group with a[scan execution policy](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/policies/scan_execution_policies/) .[Merge request approval policies](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/policies/merge_request_approval_policies/) can block merges that add a vulnerable version, and[continuous vulnerability scanning](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/dependency_scanning/continuous_dependency_scanning/) re-checks existing projects when an advisory is published, for advisories up to 14 days old.


*Figure 1: Simulated GitLab Vulnerability Report demonstrating Dependency Scanning findings for Critical and High Pillow CVEs*


1. **Container scanning** finds Ghostscript installed as an OS package. Images with Pillow but no Ghostscript cannot render EPS files, so they are lower priority. It misses Ghostscript compiled from source.[Turn container scanning on](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/application_security/container_scanning/) the same way.
2. **GitLab Orbit** : Because Pillow tends to arrive as someone else's dependency, asking "who uses it?" is hard from any single project.[GitLab Orbit](https://docs.gitlab.com/orbit/) turns your projects, pipelines, security findings and code into a graph that an agent can query. Enable it on the top-level group, then ask for the Python projects that handle images and for the projects with open findings on CVE-2026-112900 or the other Pillow advisories. This will give you a shortlist before you open a single repository.
Orbit covers only the default branch and is in beta for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed. It doesn't parse Dockerfiles yet, so confirm Ghostscript with the code search in the next step.
3. **Code search** finds what scanners miss. Run these in[exact code search](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/search/exact_code_search/) at the top-level group with regular expression mode on:


- ` file:requirements.*\\.txt$ (?i)^\\s*pillow`
- ` lang:Dockerfile (?i)ghostscript`
- ` (?i)EpsImagePlugin|\\.eps\\b`


Finally, compare the results with what actually runs. Anything running that your projects do not declare is a gap. For Kubernetes,[operational container scanning](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/clusters/agent/vulnerabilities/) covers the images in your clusters.


## Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform


Once you have the list of affected projects, the remaining work is repetitive: raise a version, open a merge request, get it reviewed. Hand the repetitive part to agents and keep people on the decisions.


Start in[Agentic Chat](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/gitlab_duo_chat/agentic_chat/) and ask it to list the Dependency Scanning findings for these Pillow CVEs from the Vulnerability Report (Ultimate), then create an epic with one issue per affected project. Assigning an issue to the[Developer Flow](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/merge_requests/developer/) produces a merge request that raises Pillow to 13.0.0 or later, or edits the version pinned in the Dockerfile. A[flow trigger](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/triggers/) on the` Assign` event starts the flow as soon as the issue is assigned. The[Code Review Flow](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/flows/foundational_flows/code_review/#automatic-reviews) can then give each merge request a first review against your[review instructions](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/duo_agent_platform/customize/review_instructions/) .


*Figure 2: Duo Agent Chat demonstrating security scanning and merge request creation to remediate Pillow vulnerabilities*


*Figure 3: Merge request created by GitLab Duo Agent Platform to remediate Pillow vulnerabilities*


The agents stop at the merge request. A person still has to review and merge each one, run the image-processing tests because 13.0.0 changes how duplicate TIFF tags and I-mode PNG saves behave, and confirm the fixed version is deployed before closing the issue.


## Timeline


Date What happened


October 16 Pillow releases[13.0.0](https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/stable/releasenotes/13.0.0.html) with fixes for 38 security entries. The release notes list the EPS Ghostscript issue as GHSA-w889-685w-c8fh with no CVE yet.


October 19 GitHub, as CNA, reserves and publishes[CVE-2026-112900](https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2026-112900) with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical). CVE-2026-112393 and CVE-2026-112403, the TIFF writer and JPEG decoder heap overflows, are published the same day.


October 20 CISA's coordinator adds an SSVC assessment for CVE-2026-112900: exploitation none, automatable yes, technical impact total.


October 23 Debian lists only its unstable release (13.0.0-1) as fixed. Ubuntu lists all releases as needing evaluation.
